learn.title: Everything is bytes
learn.body: A computer stores everything as bits, tiny switches that are either 0 or 1. Eight bits make one byte. Text, numbers, photos and programs are all long rows of bytes. To understand memory in C, you first need to read a byte.

learn.title: Binary place values
learn.body: Binary works like decimal, but each place is worth double the one before: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on. The binary number 1101 means 8 + 4 + 0 + 1, which is 13. Each place is either used (1) or not (0).

learn.title: Converting both ways
learn.body: Turn 13 into binary, then 10110 into decimal.

learn.title: A byte has a limit
learn.body: One byte holds 256 different values, 0 to 255 when unsigned. Adding 1 to 255 in an `unsigned char` wraps around to 0. For unsigned types this is defined behavior. The second line shows that the byte 65 is the letter A.
The program prints 0 and then 65 A. A byte does not know whether it is a number or a letter. The meaning comes from how your program uses it.

questions.prompt: How many different values can one byte hold?
questions.explanation: Eight bits give 2 to the power 8, which is 256 values: 0 up to 255.

questions.prompt: A byte is made of \_\_ bits.
What decimal number is the binary number 101?

questions.explanation: The fourth place from the right is worth 8, so 8 is 1000.

questions.prompt: What is the largest value an `unsigned char` can hold?
`unsigned char c = 255;` then `c = c + 1;`. What does `printf("%d\n", c)` print?
questions.explanation: A byte cannot hold 256, so an unsigned byte wraps around to 0.

questions.prompt: Match each binary number to its decimal value.
